name: Human feedback and labelling
summary: Example answers and side-by-side ratings written by people, used to teach a model to follow instructions and to prefer better answers.

D1.guide: Think first: who decides which of two answers is better?
text: After reading the library, the AI still needs to learn how to help. People write example answers to show it.
They also look at two answers side by side and pick the better one. Those choices teach the AI what people prefer.
D1.analogy: A teacher marking homework and writing model answers in the margin.

text: **Instruction data** is a set of prompts with good answers written by people, used for supervised fine-tuning.
**Preference data** shows a rater two or more model answers to the same prompt and records which is better. A reward model learns from these choices.

Who makes it: contracted annotators (often through specialist labelling firms, sometimes in lower-wage countries), paid experts such as programmers or doctors for harder topics, and users clicking thumbs up or down in apps. Increasingly, AI models do some of the rating too.

diagram.caption: How one preference label is made

D2.analogy: A teacher marking two essays and saying which one is better.
D2.analogyBreaks: A teacher can explain why. A rater often has seconds per pair, may disagree with other raters, and may prefer answers that sound confident or flattering, and the model learns those habits too.

predict.question: Raters are rushed and tend to pick the answer that sounds more confident, even when it is wrong. What will the trained model tend to do?
options: Sound confident even when it is unsure
predict.explanation: The model learns what raters reward, not what is true. Rater habits become model habits, which is one source of overconfidence and flattery (sycophancy).

text: Raters disagree, and whose preferences count is a choice with cultural and political weight. People cannot reliably grade answers to problems harder than they can solve, so feedback on expert tasks is costly and scarce.
Pay, working conditions and exposure to harmful content for annotators are ongoing concerns, and replacing people with AI raters risks copying a model's own blind spots.
